headline: High-risk filesystem-to-API workflow: Continue can read/write workspace files and use MCP, while social-auto-upload can upload media to external platforms, creating default-path prompt, leakage, and cascading-action risks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Continue can read and write workspace files and use MCP, so attacker-controlled content in shared files can influence its prompts. social-auto-upload consumes local media/account files and can act on them, creating a plausible bridge if outputs are copied into its inputs. This is not proven by docs as a default shared channel, so medium is the safer choice.
conditions: IF Continue reads instructions from workspace files that social-auto-upload can also access, injection becomes active.
IF an operator copies model output from Continue into files consumed by social-auto-upload, malicious content can steer downstream actions.
mitigations: Restrict Continue to a separate workspace folder.
Disable MCP servers that parse untrusted file content.
Use a manual review step before any file from Continue is fed into social-auto-upload.
Store social-auto-upload inputs in a dedicated directory with read-only permissions for Continue.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Continue touches source code and open editor buffers and has broad network egress, while social-auto-upload handles account data and media files. If they share a filesystem, sensitive code or account artifacts can move between them and out to external services. The profiles do not prove automatic cross-sharing, so medium fits the documented default-path risk.
conditions: IF both agents run against the same workspace directory, files can be exposed across the pair.
IF Continue sends buffer contents to a remote model provider, source code may leave the local environment.
mitigations: Separate code and media into different directories.
Use a local-only model provider for Continue.
Remove secrets from workspace files before either agent runs.
Set file permissions so social-auto-upload cannot read code directories.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Continue can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses, while social-auto-upload cannot write files or modify git state. The overlap is asymmetric, so direct write-write conflict is limited. A conflict still exists if both are pointed at the same mutable workspace, but the blast radius is mostly local file clobbering rather than shared-state corruption.
conditions: IF both agents are configured to write into the same directory, file clobbering can occur.
IF Continue subprocesses modify files that social-auto-upload later consumes, stale or partial state can be produced.
mitigations: Assign separate output directories.
Run one agent at a time when editing shared files.
Use backups or version control snapshots before writes.
Mark social-auto-upload inputs read-only during Continue sessions.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Continue can generate code or instructions, and social-auto-upload can act on local media/account files and upload to external platforms. If social-auto-upload treats Continue's output as authoritative, mistakes can cascade into incorrect uploads or account actions. No verification mechanism is documented in either profile, so the interaction is a default-path medium risk.
conditions: IF social-auto-upload consumes Continue-generated instructions without human review, errors can propagate to uploads.
IF Continue produces malformed file paths or metadata, social-auto-upload may act on them downstream.
mitigations: Require human approval before any upload.
Validate file paths and metadata against a whitelist.
Compare Continue output to source files before execution.
Use a dry-run mode for social-auto-upload when available.

E_compliance.rationale: Continue is an IDE assistant touching source code and editor buffers, while social-auto-upload handles account data and media. The profiles do not show a residency or certification mismatch, so only a limited compliance concern is visible: account/media data may be mixed with code artifacts in shared storage. The other agent is cited because the risk arises from their combined data handling.
conditions: IF account data is stored in the same workspace as source code, retention and access controls may diverge.
IF either agent logs file contents to external services, policy obligations may differ by data class.
mitigations: Separate account-data storage from code repositories.
Review retention settings for both tools.
Avoid placing personal media in the coding workspace.
Document which data classes each agent may process.
